extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners, patent practitioners, applicants, and patent law students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating patent claims for novelty (35 U.S.C. 102) and obviousness (35 U.S.C. 103), including what counts as prior art, how to apply anticipation and obviousness standards, relevant factual inquiries, and common rebuttals and examples. Geared to examination and prosecution contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Prior Art
rubrics_metrics.description: References — Printed Documents, including Patents and Published Patent Applications (Domestic and Foreign) and Other Printed Publications (Non‑Patent Literature), such as magazine, newspaper articles, electronic publication, including on‑line databases, websites, or Internet publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP 2126‑2128. Prior art includes printed publications and patent documents; electronic and internet publications qualify. Examiner should consider these sources when searching and applying 102/103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's Admissions of Prior Art (AAPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements made by applicant that certain information was 'prior art' (may appear in the background, drawings, or remarks) which are admissions that that work is available as prior art against applicant's claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP 2129 and MPEP 706.02 III. When material is labeled/ described as 'prior art', the examiner must determine whether the subject matter identified is applicant's own work or the work of another; admissions can be used even if the material wouldn't otherwise qualify under statutory categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation / Lack of Novelty (35 U.S.C. 102)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 35 U.S.C. 102, prior art is used to establish lack of novelty, commonly referred to as 'anticipation' — when a single prior art reference teaches each and every element of a claim, either expressly or inherently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim lacks novelty when it is anticipated by a single reference. Examiner must identify that each claim element is disclosed in the single reference (expressly or inherently).

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) — Disclosure with Prior Public Availability Date
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure that is publicly available before the effective filing date can serve as prior art under 102(a)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include public disclosures, publications, internet postings that have a public availability date prior to the effective filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) — U.S. Patent, U.S. Patent Application, and PCT with Prior Filing Date
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. patents, U.S. patent applications, and PCT applications having an earlier effective filing date can be prior art under 102(a)(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These references are treated as prior art based on their earlier effective filing dates; consider priority chains and filing dates when applying this provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102(b) — Exceptions / Grace Periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Exceptions to what constitutes a basis for rejection under 102(b), including grace period disclosures by the inventor or disclosures obtained from the inventor, intervening third‑party disclosures, and commonly owned disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand and apply the statutory exceptions (e.g., inventor's own disclosures, disclosures obtained from inventor, intervening disclosures, commonly owned disclosures) when deciding whether a reference is a proper basis for rejection. See diagram on 102(a)/(b) interplay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness Legal Standard (35 U.S.C. 103)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may not be obtained if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date to a person having ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA); patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a legal conclusion based on underlying factual inquiries; apply the Graham factors and relevant case law (e.g., KSR) when determining obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to Use a 35 U.S.C. 103 Rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a 103 rejection when the claimed invention is not identically disclosed (so not an anticipation), and the reference teachings must be modified or combined to meet the claims; the differences must have been obvious at the time to a PHOSITA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether modifications would have been obvious to PHOSITA at the time of invention; see MPEP §706.02. 103 applies where claims require combining/ modifying reference teachings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims Must Be Viewed as a Whole
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining differences between prior art and the claims, the question under 35 U.S.C. 103 is whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious—not whether individual differences would have been obvious in isolation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dissect the claim into parts for the obviousness inquiry; consider the claimed combination and reference Stratoflex v. Aeroquip for authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person Having Ordinary Skill in the Art (PHOSITA)
rubrics_metrics.description: PHOSITA is a hypothetical person whose skill level depends upon the technical field; PHOSITA's skill level may not be the same as the examiner or the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define PHOSITA for the particular field when analyzing obviousness; this is fact‑specific and affects obviousness determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham v. John Deere — Core Obviousness Inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: The Graham inquiries: (1) Scope and content of the prior art; (2) Differences between the prior art and the claims; (3) Level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art at the time of the invention; (4) Does any objective evidence of nonobviousness (secondary considerations) exist?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these four factual inquiries as the framework for analyzing obviousness; support conclusions with articulated reasoning and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary Considerations / Objective Evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary considerations that bear on nonobviousness include unexpected results, long‑felt need/failure of others, commercial success, copying by others, inoperability of prior art, and skepticism of experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider these objective indicia as rebuttal evidence to a prima facie case of obviousness; they can be decisive if supported by substantial evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining Level of Ordinary Skill in the Art
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors to determine the level of ordinary skill include types of problems encountered in the art, prior art solutions, rapidity of innovation, sophistication of the technology, and educational level of active workers in the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all factors are necessary in every case; examiners may rely on their technical expertise to describe PHOSITA's knowledge and skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim Interpretation Standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are given their broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This interpretation determines the examiner's search scope. See In re Abbott Diabetes Care Inc., 104 USPQ2d 1337 (Fed. Cir. 2012) for guidance; structural similarity between prior art and invention is not required if similar utility exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale Requirement (KSR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness rejections cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements; there must be articulated reasoning with a rational underpinning to support the legal conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite KSR: 'there must be some articulated reasoning with some rational underpinning'—provide specific explanation why a PHOSITA would combine or modify references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining References for a 103 Rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: A 103 rejection may be based on a combination of references; a single reference need not teach all aspects of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When combining references, articulate the motivation or reason to combine and show interrelated teachings, market/design pressure, background knowledge of PHOSITA as explained in KSR. Provide a rationale for the combination rather than conclusory assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: What to Search For
rubrics_metrics.description: Search for the claimed subject matter and also for prior art related to disclosed features which might reasonably be expected to be claimed (MPEP §904.02).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer references that provide a teaching or suggestion to combine claimed elements (see MPEP §2141). Look for references that would have given a PHOSITA a reason to combine elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous Prior Art
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art is analogous if it is from the field of endeavor at the time of invention or otherwise logically would have commended itself to an inventor's attention in considering the invention as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners are not limited to the applicant's field; use references from other fields that a PHOSITA would recognize as useful. See KSR and MPEP §2141.01(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's Rebuttal Arguments Against Obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Common rebuttals include arguments that elements are not combinable, destruction of the reference, the combination works differently than individual elements, the prior art fails to teach an element, and that the art is non‑analogous. Impermissible hindsight is also a concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are non‑exclusive examples; examiners should address such arguments substantively. A good examiner response shows why the rebuttal does not overcome the articulated rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishing a Prima Facie Case of Obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The key to supporting any 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection is clear articulation of the rationale or reasons why the claimed invention would have been obvious; mere conclusory statements are not adequate. A prima facie case requires a reasonable expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If proposed modifications would render the invention inoperable or change its principle of operation, a prima facie case cannot be established. Cite In re Kahn and KSR guidance (In re Kahn, 78 USPQ2d 1329).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modifications That Prevent a Prima Facie Case
rubrics_metrics.description: If a proposed modification of a prior art invention would render it inoperable or unsatisfactory for its intended purpose, or would change its principle of operation, then a prima facie case of obviousness cannot be established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the modification would make the reference inoperable or alter its operating principle; if so, that weighs against a 103 rejection. Also require reasonable expectation of success for obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching Away and Unexpected (Non‑Predictable) Results
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed combination may be nonobvious where the prior art teaches away from the claimed combination and the combination yields more than predictable results (e.g., Crocs — foam strap contacting foam base produced unexpected comfort/result).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if elements are individually known, teaching away or unpredictable synergistic results can support nonobviousness. Use factual findings about predictability and prior art attitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substituting One Known Element for Another (Predictable Variation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that is a simple substitution of one art‑recognized element for another (with well‑known, predictable function) is likely obvious (Agrizap example substituting resistive electrical switch for mechanical switch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the substitution was routine for PHOSITA and whether the substituted element's function was predictable; predictable, routine substitutions support obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims Define the Invention and Require Whole‑Claim Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed invention defines what applicant believes is the invention; claims must be considered as a whole and the analysis should include the problem being solved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dissecting claims into isolated parts; analyze similarities/differences in structure and function relative to prior art and consider analogous vs non‑analogous art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference Between Federal Courts and Patent Office Processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal courts address infringement and validity and are not flexible (cannot amend patents); the Patent Office addresses patentability and prosecution is flexible (allowing give and take to determine appropriate claim scope), permits amendments by applicant, accepts rebuttal arguments, and considers secondary considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize procedural and remedial differences between court litigation and USPTO examination/prosecution contexts when framing rejections and responses.
